# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Clinical and Evidence-Based Review

## Introduction and Rationale
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major contributor to ischemic stroke, with the left atrial appendage (LAA) harboring over 90% of stroke-inducing thrombi in non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) [1]. The standard of care for stroke prevention in NVAF is oral anticoagulation (OAC), using either vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). However, long-term OAC has major clinical limitations, including high bleeding risks, lifestyle-limiting side effects, and poor long-term adherence [2]. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a safe and effective non-pharmacological alternative for patients seeking mitigation of stroke risk without the attendant hazards of lifelong systemic anticoagulation.

## Clinical Evidence from Landmark Trials
Pivotal evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of LAAC initially emerged from the PROTECT AF and PREVAIL trials [2,3]. These randomized clinical trials evaluated the first-generation Watchman device against warfarin [4,5]. Long-term five-year data from these trials demonstrated that LAAC provides comparable stroke prevention to warfarin, with significant reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality [6]. 

While early trials compared LAAC with warfarin, contemporary clinical practice has shifted toward comparing LAAC directly with DOACs. The PRAGUE-17 trial, a randomized multi-center study comparing LAAC (utilizing primarily the Amplatzer Amulet or Watchman devices) with DOACs, demonstrated that LAAC was non-inferior to DOACs regarding the composite primary endpoint of major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events [7]. This non-inferiority was sustained at four years, highlighted by a notable reduction in non-procedural clinically significant bleeding [8].

## Device Advancements and Registries
Technology has rapidly evolved to optimize occlusion and procedural safety. The next-generation Watchman FLX device, evaluated in the PINNACLE FLX trial, showed exceptionally high implant success (98.8%) and extremely low rates of perioperative complications, such as pericardial effusion or device embolization [9]. Similarly, the Amplatzer Amulet device offers a dual-mode mechanism (disc and lobe) to "seal and plug" the LAA. The AMULET IDE trial directly compared the Amulet with the first-generation Watchman, demonstrating the Amulet's non-inferiority in safety and efficacy, while achieving superior LAA occlusion rates and fewer residual peri-device leaks (PDL) [10].

Large-scale clinical registries have corroborated these findings, proving high procedural success in diverse, real-world cohorts. The EWOLUTION registry evaluated the Watchman device in high-bleeding-risk patients, demonstrating excellent long-term efficacy and safety [11]. Observational studies and registries focusing on the Amplatzer devices have shown similarly high procedural success rates and low complication profiles [12,13]. Other devices, such as the LAmbre system, have also shown utility, particularly in complex, multi-lobed, or shallow LAA anatomies [14].

## Imaging and Procedural Management
Accurate pre-procedural sizing and intra-procedural guidance are paramount to procedural success [15]. While transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the standard diagnostic method, multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) is increasingly used for 3D sizing and planning [16]. Intra-procedurally, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) is emerging as a preferred alternative to TEE in many centers, eliminating the need for general anesthesia and reducing esophageal trauma without compromising device sizing or safety [17,18].

## Complications and Post-Procedural Care
Despite technical advances, challenges remain. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 2% to 4% of patients and is associated with an elevated risk of subsequent ischemic stroke [19,20]. Tailored antithrombotic therapies are necessary to prevent and manage DRT [21]. Another challenge is residual peri-device leak (PDL). Large PDLs (>5 mm) have long been considered clinically significant, but recent data suggest that even minor residual leaks (1–3 mm) may increase thromboembolic risk, underscoring the necessity of complete closure [22].

In patients with absolute contraindications to OAC, the ASAP registry demonstrated the safety and efficacy of LAAC using post-procedural dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) [23]. Post-LAAC antithrombotic regimens continue to evolve; real-world data from the EWOLUTION registry and collaborative analyses suggest that direct-to-DAPT or short-term DOAC strategies are safe and effective alternatives [24,25]. Multi-center analyses confirm that newer devices lower PDL risk while optimizing outcomes [26,27].

## Guidelines and Future Directions
The clinical role of LAA exclusion is further reinforced by surgical evidence, such as the LAAOS III trial, which showed that surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery significantly reduces stroke [28]. Currently, international guidelines recommend LAAC (Class IIb) for stroke prevention in patients with NVAF and contraindications to long-term OAC [29]. Registry data, including the US NCDR LAAO registry, continue to show excellent real-world outcomes and low complication rates [30]. Ongoing trials will clarify whether LAAC can serve as a first-line alternative to DOACs in broader patient populations.
